h1: Planning a batch of homebrew for a house party
title: Planning Homebrew for a House Party | Craft Beer School
desc: How to plan a homebrew batch for a party: choosing a style, timing the brew, working out quantities, serving it cold and keeping it responsible.
teaser: Brewing for a party is a lovely idea that goes wrong when the beer is still fermenting on the day. Work backwards from the date.
standfirst: Serving your own beer at a party is one of the best rewards of homebrewing. Here is how to pick a style, time the brew so it is ready, work out how much to make and serve it well and responsibly.
sections:
The most common mistake is starting too late. Beer needs time to ferment, condition and carbonate. As a rough guide for an ale:

  • Fermentation: 1 to 2 weeks.
  • Conditioning on the yeast: a few extra days to a week.
  • Carbonation: about 2 weeks in bottles, or a few days to a week in a keg.

That means at least four weeks for a bottled ale. Six is safer. Lagers need much longer. Our guide on how long beer takes to ferment covers the details. Put the brew day in your calendar six weeks before the party, not three.

A party is not the time for an experiment. Pick a beer that:

  • is ready quickly, without long ageing.
  • appeals to people who do not usually drink craft beer.
  • is moderate in strength, around 4 to 5% ABV.
  • you have brewed successfully before.

Pale ales, wheat beers and blonde ales are reliable choices. A light wheat beer pairs well with Indian snacks like pakoras, chaat and grilled paneer tikka. If you ferment without temperature control in warm weather, a saison or a kveik-fermented pale ale tolerates the heat better than most styles.

A standard 20 litre batch, once you leave sediment behind, gives about 18 to 19 litres. That is roughly 55 bottles of 330 ml or 28 bottles of 650 ml.

Plan for modest servings. A small glass of 250 to 330 ml per person for a couple of rounds is generous for a house party, with plenty of non-alcoholic drinks alongside. One full batch comfortably covers 15 to 25 guests who are also drinking other things. If you need more, brew two smaller batches of different styles rather than one huge one. Our guide to scaling a beer recipe shows how to adjust quantities.

Bottles are easy to share and need no special equipment. They take longer to carbonate and leave you with a lot of glass to wash afterwards.

A keg is quicker to carbonate, easier to serve and makes a pleasant focal point. It needs a CO2 cylinder, a regulator and a way to keep it cold. Mini kegs of 5 litres are a good middle ground for small parties. Our guide to kegging homebrew covers the set-up.

In Indian weather, keeping beer cold is half the battle. A day before the party:

  • Chill bottles or the keg in the fridge so the beer is at serving temperature and the sediment settles.
  • Have a big tub or cooler with ice and a little water ready for bottles once guests arrive. Ice water chills faster than ice alone.
  • Pour bottle-conditioned beer carefully, leaving the last centimetre of yeast in the bottle. Or show guests how.

Cold crashing the fermenter for a couple of days before bottling or kegging helps the beer pour clearer. Here is one practical detail worth stealing from a commercial taproom: test pour two or three days before the party. If the beer is flat, cloudy or tastes young, you still have time to fix carbonation or chill it longer.

A good host looks after guests as well as the beer:

  • Offer plenty of non-alcoholic drinks and good food alongside.
  • Label each beer with its strength, so people know what they are drinking.
  • Use small glasses rather than pint mugs.
  • Never let anyone drive after drinking. Arrange cabs or a sober driver ahead of time.
  • Do not serve anyone under the legal drinking age in your state.

Rules on making and serving alcohol at home vary by state in India and change over time. Check the current position where you live. Homebrew is for sharing with friends, never for selling.

Ask a few people what they thought. Party feedback is less precise than a proper tasting, but it tells you which beers people went back for. Write it in your brew log alongside the recipe.

Timing a batch for a party teaches you to plan fermentation and conditioning to a date. Learning to control those stages, so the beer is ready when you need it and tastes the way you planned, is what moves a homebrewer from lucky batches to reliable ones.
faqs: How far in advance should I brew for a party?
At least four weeks for a bottled ale and six to be safe. Kegged beer can be ready a little sooner. Lagers need much longer.
How much beer does a 20 litre batch make?
About 18 to 19 litres after leaving the sediment behind, which is roughly 55 bottles of 330 ml or 28 of 650 ml.
What beer style is best for a party?
A moderate-strength pale ale, wheat beer or blonde ale that is ready quickly and appeals to people who do not usually drink craft beer.
